## The question

Philadelphia is a city of both renters and homeowners, and the balance between them changes from neighborhood to neighborhood. In this analysis, I predict the **share of occupied housing units that are renter-occupied** in each census tract. I start with a baseline model built from the American Community Survey, add spatial features built from the city's open data portal, and transform variables. I keep a model log the whole way through to see which changes actually lower out-of-sample error.

---

## Part 0: Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""
```

Every model is cross-validated with the helper below. It runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in the log is tested on the same folds. It stops if any variable in the formula has missing values, so no rows are dropped by accident.

```{r}
#| label: cv-helper
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}
```

```{r}
#| label: log-start
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)
```

---

## Part 1: Choosing the outcome

### 1A: Pulling the outcome and baseline predictors

My outcome is the renter share: renter-occupied units (`B25003_003`) divided by all occupied units (`B25003_001`). For the baseline, I use four ACS predictors that plausibly relate to whether households rent: median household income, median age, average household size, and the share of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher. I leave out housing-type variables such as units in structure (`B25024`), because the number of apartments in a building measures tenure almost directly, which would be leakage.

```{r}
#| label: pull
philly_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(
    total_pop   = "B01003_001",
    occ_units   = "B25003_001",   # occupied housing units
    renter_occ  = "B25003_003",   # renter-occupied units
    med_inc     = "B19013_001",   # median household income
    med_age     = "B01002_001",   # median age
    avg_hh_size = "B25010_001",   # average household size
    edu_total   = "B15003_001",   # population 25+
    ba          = "B15003_022",
    ma          = "B15003_023",
    prof        = "B15003_024",
    phd         = "B15003_025"
  ),
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(2272)
```

Because the outcome is a proportion, I use `moe_prop()` for its margin of error rather than the MOE of the renter count. I then calculate the coefficient of variation (CV) from the standard error.

```{r}
#| label: build-outcome
philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    y = case_when(
      occ_unitsE > 0 ~ renter_occE / occ_unitsE * 100,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    y_moe = case_when(
      occ_unitsE > 0 ~ moe_prop(renter_occE, occ_unitsE, renter_occM, occ_unitsM) * 100,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    y_cv = case_when(
      y > 0 ~ (y_moe / 1.645) / y * 100,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    med_inc     = med_incE,
    med_age     = med_ageE,
    avg_hh_size = avg_hh_sizeE,
    pct_ba      = case_when(
      edu_totalE > 0 ~ (baE + maE + profE + phdE) / edu_totalE * 100,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )
```

### 1B: Is it reliable enough to model?

I classify CV values below 12% as reliable, 12%–40% as somewhat reliable, and above 40% as unreliable.

```{r}
#| label: reliability
sum(is.na(philly_tracts$y))

summary(philly_tracts$y_cv)

philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    is.na(y_cv) ~ "Unavailable",
    y_cv < 12   ~ "Reliable",
    y_cv <= 40  ~ "Somewhat reliable",
    TRUE        ~ "Unreliable"
  )) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(reliability)

ggplot(philly_tracts, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Renter share across Philadelphia tracts",
    subtitle = "2019–2023 ACS",
    x = "Renter-occupied units (%)",
    y = "Number of tracts"
  )
```

The renter share is built from large counts, because every occupied unit is either owned or rented. Of the 408 tracts, 20 have no value for the outcome. The median tract CV is 15.1%: 111 tracts are reliable, 271 are somewhat reliable, only 5 are unreliable, and 21 have no calculable CV. Five unreliable tracts is about 1% of the tracts with a CV, far below the one-third threshold, so the outcome is reliable enough to model. Unreliable estimates are concentrated in tracts where very few households rent, because a small share is divided into a similar-sized margin of error. The city's Division of Housing and Community Development would want to predict this outcome to target tenant protection programs, such as eviction diversion and rental repair assistance, toward the neighborhoods where renters live.

### 1C: Deciding which tracts to model

I filter once here, and every later step uses `tracts`.

```{r}
#| label: filter
tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  filter(total_popE > 0,
         !is.na(y),
         !is.na(med_inc),
         !is.na(med_age),
         !is.na(avg_hh_size),
         !is.na(pct_ba))

nrow(philly_tracts)
nrow(tracts)
```

I lose 27 of 408 tracts, leaving 381 to model. These are places with no residents or households, such as Fairmount Park, the airport, and industrial land along the rivers, plus a few institutional tracts where median income is suppressed. None of them contains a meaningful number of renter households.

---

## Part 2: Baseline model

### 2A: Looking first

```{r}
#| label: look
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = med_inc, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Median household income", y = "Renter-occupied units (%)")

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = med_age, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Median age", y = "Renter-occupied units (%)")

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = avg_hh_size, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Average household size", y = "Renter-occupied units (%)")

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = pct_ba, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Adults with a bachelor's degree or higher (%)", y = "Renter-occupied units (%)")
```

### 2B: Fitting and logging the baseline

```{r}
#| label: m1
f1 <- y ~ med_inc + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba

m1 <- lm(f1, data = tracts)
summary(m1)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m1", added = "ACS baseline",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f1, tracts),
          notes = "income, median age, household size, % BA+")

model_log
```

On tracts it hasn't seen, the baseline model misses the renter share by about 13.4 percentage points. Its in-sample R² is 0.58, so the four ACS variables already explain a good share of the variation.

### 2C: Where the baseline is wrong

```{r}
#| label: resid-map-1
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(resid_m1 = residuals(m1))

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m1), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Baseline model: where it's wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = more renters than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")
```

The residuals are not randomly scattered. The clearest blue cluster (fewer renters than predicted) runs along the Delaware River north of Center City, and there are more blue tracts in parts of the Northwest. Red tracts (more renters than predicted) cluster in South Philadelphia, including the large tract along the southern Delaware waterfront, in Manayunk and Roxborough on the northwest edge of the city, and in parts of the lower Northeast. These places differ in their housing and neighborhood conditions more than in who lives there. Along the Delaware, long-time homeowners likely live next to newer, highly educated residents, so the model expects more renters than there are; in South Philadelphia and Manayunk, many rowhomes are rented to young adults. The baseline also does not know where students live or about neighborhood conditions beyond median income. I therefore pull university campuses, residential burglaries, and shootings in Part 3.

---

## Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia's open data portal

```{r}
#| label: carto-helper
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}
```

I pull three layers, all from 2023 or earlier, so no information comes from after the outcome's time window. I count records with no location and drop them.

```{r}
#| label: my-layers
# Layer 1: residential burglaries, 2023
burglary <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, text_general_code, dispatch_date
   FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
     AND text_general_code = 'Burglary Residential'"
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

nrow(burglary)
sum(st_is_empty(burglary))
burglary <- burglary %>% filter(!st_is_empty(burglary))

# Layer 2: shooting victims, 2023
shootings <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, date_
   FROM shootings
   WHERE date_ >= '2023-01-01' AND date_ < '2024-01-01'"
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

nrow(shootings)
sum(st_is_empty(shootings))
shootings <- shootings %>% filter(!st_is_empty(shootings))

# Layer 3: university and college campuses
universities <- st_read("https://hub.arcgis.com/api/v3/datasets/8ad76bc179cf44bd9b1c23d6f66f57d1_0/downloads/data?format=geojson&spatialRefId=4326&where=1%3D1") %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

nrow(universities)
sum(st_is_empty(universities))
universities <- universities %>% filter(!st_is_empty(universities))
```

I lose 119 of 3,800 burglary records and 1 of 1,673 shooting records because they have no location. The campus file has 644 features, and none is missing a location.

All three layers follow from the Part 2C map. University campuses capture student housing, which drives renting in a way that median age and education only partly describe. The campus file is updated as needed rather than by year, but the campuses existed long before 2023, so it does not bring in information from the future. Residential burglaries and shootings stand in for neighborhood conditions and disinvestment that median income misses. None of these layers is built from tenure, so none is leakage.

---

## Part 4: Building spatial features

### 4A: Counting and density

Counts are divided by tract area, because raw counts mostly measure tract size.

```{r}
#| label: density
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi          = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
    n_burglary         = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)),
    burglary_per_sqmi  = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    n_shootings        = lengths(st_intersects(., shootings)),
    shootings_per_sqmi = n_shootings / area_sqmi
  )

summary(tracts$burglary_per_sqmi)
summary(tracts$shootings_per_sqmi)
```

### 4B: Distance to the nearest campus

```{r}
#| label: nearest
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, universities)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_univ_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, universities[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

summary(tracts$dist_univ_mi)
```

### 4C: Distance to City Hall

```{r}
#| label: city-hall
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)

summary(tracts$dist_ch_mi)
```

### 4D: Adding the features one at a time

```{r}
#| label: my-spatial
f2 <- y ~ med_inc + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba + dist_univ_mi

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "distance to nearest campus",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
          notes = "nearest distance")

f3 <- y ~ med_inc + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba + dist_univ_mi +
  burglary_per_sqmi

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "burglary density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
          notes = "2023 residential burglaries per sq mi")

f4 <- y ~ med_inc + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba + dist_univ_mi +
  burglary_per_sqmi + shootings_per_sqmi

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "shooting density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
          notes = "2023 shooting victims per sq mi")

f5 <- y ~ med_inc + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba + dist_univ_mi +
  burglary_per_sqmi + shootings_per_sqmi + dist_ch_mi

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m5", added = "distance to City Hall",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f5, tracts),
          notes = "distance to one place")

model_log
```

None of the spatial features improved much on the baseline. Burglary density was the only one that lowered CV RMSE, from 13.45 (m2) to 13.38 (m3), likely because residential burglaries are most common where housing is dense and many units sit close together, which is where renters live. Even so, m3 did not beat the baseline's 13.35. The feature that helped least was distance to the nearest campus, which raised CV RMSE from 13.35 to 13.45. The campus file contains 644 separate features, including small buildings spread across the city, so most tracts are close to some campus feature and the distance does not single out student neighborhoods. Median age and the share of adults with a degree already capture much of the student effect. Shooting density (13.40) and distance to City Hall (13.43) also added nothing as straight-line terms, likely because income and education already describe the same neighborhood differences.

---

## Part 5: Transforming features

I keep the outcome untransformed so every row in the log stays in percentage points.

### 5A: Logs

```{r}
#| label: log-look
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = med_inc)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()
```

Income and both densities are right-skewed. I use `log()` for income, which is never 0 after the filter, and `log1p()` for the densities, which can be 0.

```{r}
#| label: m-log
f_log <- y ~ log(med_inc) + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba + dist_univ_mi +
  log1p(burglary_per_sqmi) + log1p(shootings_per_sqmi) + dist_ch_mi

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m6", added = "log of income and both densities",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_log, tracts),
          notes = "log() for income; log1p() for densities")
```

### 5B: Squared term

```{r}
#| label: squared-plot
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: m-squared
f_sq <- y ~ log(med_inc) + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba + dist_univ_mi +
  log1p(burglary_per_sqmi) + log1p(shootings_per_sqmi) + dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m7", added = "squared distance to City Hall",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_sq, tracts),
          notes = "m6 + I(dist_ch_mi^2)")
```

### 5C: Categorical variable

```{r}
#| label: m-categorical
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)

f_cat <- y ~ log(med_inc) + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba + dist_univ_mi +
  log1p(burglary_per_sqmi) + log1p(shootings_per_sqmi) + dist_ch_mi + ring

m_cat <- lm(f_cat, data = tracts)
summary(m_cat)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m8", added = "ring (Core / Inner / Outer)",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_cat, tracts),
          notes = "m6 + ring; reference = Core")

model_log
```

The transformation that helped most was the log, which lowered CV RMSE from 13.43 (m5) to 13.11 (m6). Adding the squared distance to City Hall lowered it further to 12.96 (m7), while the ring categories barely changed it (13.09 in m8, compared with 13.11 in m6). For the ring variable, the reference level is Core, tracts within 2 miles of City Hall. Holding the other variables in m8 constant, an Outer-ring tract has a predicted renter share about 6.5 percentage points lower than a Core tract.

---

## Part 6: The final model

I keep the features and transformations that lowered CV RMSE in the model log, judged by CV RMSE rather than p-values. The final model is m7, which has the lowest CV RMSE (12.96). I drop the ring categories because they lowered CV RMSE by only 0.02 in m8 and overlap with the distance terms. I keep all four spatial features: on their own they did not help, but with the logs and the squared term they are part of the model with the lowest out-of-sample error.

```{r}
#| label: final
f_final <- y ~ log(med_inc) + med_age + avg_hh_size + pct_ba + dist_univ_mi +
  log1p(burglary_per_sqmi) + log1p(shootings_per_sqmi) + dist_ch_mi +
  I(dist_ch_mi^2)

m_final <- lm(f_final, data = tracts)
summary(m_final)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "final", added = "same as m7",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_final, tracts),
          notes = "logs + squared distance to City Hall; ring dropped")

model_log
```

### Where the final model is wrong

```{r}
#| label: resid-map-2
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(resid_final = residuals(m_final))

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_final), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Final model: where it's wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = more renters than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")

sd(tracts$resid_m1)
sd(tracts$resid_final)
```

Compared with the baseline map in Part 2C, the final model's errors are smaller overall: the standard deviation of the residuals falls from 13.3 to 12.6 percentage points. The blue strip along the Delaware River north of Center City and the red tract on the southern Delaware waterfront both fade. Red clusters stay in Manayunk and Roxborough and in parts of the lower Northeast, and some blue tracts remain in the Northwest.

### Are the biggest misses in the least reliable tracts?

```{r}
#| label: fog
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = y_cv, y = abs(resid_final))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the renter-share estimate (%)", y = "Size of the miss") +
  theme_minimal()

cor(tracts$y_cv, abs(tracts$resid_final), use = "complete.obs")
mean(abs(tracts$resid_final) < tracts$y_moe, na.rm = TRUE)
```

---

## Part 7: Reflection

My baseline model, built from income, median age, household size, and education, missed the renter share by about 13.4 percentage points on tracts it had not seen. The final model lowers that to 13.0, a modest gain of about 0.4 points. The most surprising part of the model log was that the spatial features barely helped. Burglary density was the only one that lowered CV RMSE, likely because burglaries concentrate where housing is dense. The most disappointing was distance to the nearest campus, which made predictions worse, likely because the campus file includes many small buildings spread across the city and the ACS variables already capture students through age and education. Most of the gain came from transformations instead: logging income and the densities, and letting distance to City Hall curve. The model log showed me that a variable can look important on a map and still add little once related variables are in the model.

Take median age. The β̂ reading is that, holding the other variables constant, a tract whose median age is 10 years older has a predicted renter share about 9.4 percentage points lower (a coefficient of −0.94 per year); this is an association, not evidence that aging causes people to buy homes. The ŷ reading is that median age stays in the model because it carries information about tenure that lowers out-of-sample error, whether or not the relationship is causal.

The final residual map still shows clusters in Manayunk and Roxborough and in parts of the lower Northeast, where there are more renters than predicted. Next I would measure the age and size of the housing stock, using building age and lot size from the Office of Property Assessment's property data, because older, subdivided rowhomes are often rented even where incomes are moderate. I would also add college enrollment from the ACS (table B14007) to separate student renters from long-term renters.

The last plot shows almost no relationship between the reliability of the estimate and the size of the miss. Large misses occur at every level of CV, some of the largest are in tracts with reliable estimates, and the correlation between the two is only about 0.06. At the same time, for about 60% of tracts the final model's miss is smaller than the outcome's own 90% margin of error, so the model cannot be judged wrong there. Survey noise is part of the remaining error, but the largest misses look like a modeling problem rather than fog.
